subject: Computing

unit.unitOverview:
The first idea is the algorithm. An algorithm is just a set of instructions in the right order. The second idea is the program. When we write our algorithm as blocks that a computer can follow, we have made a program. The third idea is debugging. A mistake in a program is called a bug. Finding it and fixing it is called debugging — and it is much faster and more fun when we work with a friend.

The free tool for this unit is ScratchJr. The source textbook names ScratchJr directly, so we use exactly the tool it intends. This is a colourful app made especially for you aged five to seven, so it is a perfect fit for Year 2. There is no reading of code and no typing — you simply drag picture blocks together and tap the green flag to see their character move. You join blocks like Start on Green Flag, Hop, Turn Right and Move Right to bring a dancer to life.
learningPath: Preview the goals, key words and the tools you will use
Read the concept explainers and study the code examples
Follow the methods and worked examples
Build the activities, debug your work and play the games
Apply, explain and finish the Unit Project and Challenge

provenance.transformation: Structured from the Cambridge Primary Computing 0672 — Stage 2 Teacher & Parent Guide, Activity Sheet and Mini-Project. Teacher-directed prose was rewritten into learner-facing explainers so the unit teaches with no adult present.

outcomes: Follow and understand an algorithm — a set of instructions in the correct order.
Explain, in their own words, why the order of the steps matters.
Plan instructions for a character by writing a simple dance algorithm.
Turn an algorithm into a program in ScratchJr using blocks such as Start on Green Flag, Hop, Turn Right and Move Right.
Add a second character that starts to dance using the Start on Bump block.
Say what a bug is, and debug a short program by finding and fixing one mistake.
Explain why it is helpful to work with others when debugging.
Run a program with the green flag and check whether it did what they wanted.

concepts.title: Algorithms: putting the moves in the right order (unplugged)
concepts.explanation:
An algorithm is a set of instructions in the right order. If the order is wrong, the instructions do not work. A dance is a lovely example: the moves must come in the right order or the dance falls apart.

Stand up together and say: “Let us do a little dance! First we HOP. Then we TURN around. Then we STEP to the side.” Do it as a class, calling the moves in order. Now do it in a silly, muddled order — “Step, hop, turn. no wait, turn, step, hop!” — and you can giggle at how it goes wrong.
concepts.example: When we put the moves in the right order, that is called an algorithm. Computers need their instructions in the right order too.
concepts.checkYourself: you cannot land before you jump. Can you put the moves in an order that makes sense?

concepts.title: Meet ScratchJr: make a character move
concepts.explanation:
Today we open ScratchJr and meet the blocks. Blocks are picture instructions. We drag them together to make a character move. The yellow Start on Green Flag block starts everything when we tap the green flag.

tap the blue plus to add a character (a person). The yellow blocks start things.
concepts.example: The blue blocks make our character move. Open a new project and tap the picture button at the top to choose a Background.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you drag and snap two or three blocks together and run the program with the green flag? Can you point to the green-flag block and say it starts the program? Can you add a background and a character?

concepts.title: Design a dance: from algorithm to program
concepts.explanation:
Now we are real designers. First we plan the dance as an algorithm (the moves in order).

Try it: Support you to plan on paper first, then build.

Check yourself: Can you run it and say whether it did what you wanted? Can you add a Start on Bump character? Do you build the blocks in the same order as the plan?
concepts.example: Then we turn the algorithm into a program by dragging the matching blocks in ScratchJr. Same order on paper, same order in the app.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you run it and say whether it did what you wanted? Can you add a Start on Bump character? Do you build the blocks in the same order as the plan?

concepts.title: Bugs and debugging: fixing it together
concepts.explanation:
A bug is a mistake in a program. Finding and fixing it is called debugging. Everyone makes bugs — even the best programmers — so debugging is a normal, happy part of the job. And it is faster and easier with a friend: two pairs of eyes find the mistake sooner.

A bug is just a mistake in our instructions. When we find it and fix it, we are debugging. It is like proofreading a story to find the letter that is wrong.
concepts.example: Find one real example of bugs and debugging: fixing it together around you, or on a device you use. Say out loud what it is and why it fits.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you understand that a bug is a mistake we can fix, not a disaster? Can you work kindly with a partner to find it? Can you find one wrong block and say what it should be?

concepts.title: Be a designer: the Mini-Project
concepts.explanation:
This session and the Mini-Project go hand in hand. Now you are the designer. You will make a dancer for our Ehel Academy celebration.

Try it: You complete the — plan a dance, build it with two characters (one using Start on Bump), find and fix the bug in with a partner, and then make it better with one extra block.

Check yourself: Does your program run and roughly match your plan? Did you find and fix the bug in Part C? Did you work well with your partner? Do you plan before building?
concepts.example: First plan your moves, then build them, then check it works — and if there is a bug, find it with your partner. Keep routines short — three or four moves is plenty.
concepts.checkYourself: Does your program run and roughly match your plan? Did you find and fix the bug in Part C? Did you work well with your partner? Do you plan before building?

Did You Know?
A mistake in a program is called a bug. Long ago, a real moth flew into a big computer and stopped it working — a real bug!
A space robot once had a bug in its program and could not finish its trip to Mars. That is why we always check our code!

debugging.symptom: Your program runs but does the wrong thing.
debugging.cause: The instructions are in the wrong order, or one is missing.
debugging.fix: Read your steps out loud one at a time and act them out. The first step that does not match what you wanted is the bug.

debugging.symptom: Nothing happens when you run it.
debugging.cause: There is no trigger, or the blocks are not joined together.
debugging.fix: Check that your first block is a start block and that every block below it is snapped on.
Put the steps that should happen again inside a repeat or forever loop.

esafety.title: Check before you trust
esafety.text: Anyone can put anything on the internet, so not everything you read is true. Check an important fact on a second, different website, and ask an adult you trust if you are not sure.

esafety.title: Tell someone if something worries you
esafety.text: If anything online upsets you, or someone asks you for personal information or to keep a secret, stop, leave the page and tell an adult you trust straight away. It is never your fault.

esafety.title: Respect other people's work
esafety.text: Pictures, music and writing belong to whoever made them. Use work that is free to use, and say where you got it. Your own work belongs to you — put your name on it.

commonMistakes: It matters a lot. The same moves in a different order make a different dance — and some orders do not work at all (you cannot land before you jump). Show a muddled version to prove it.
A bug means I am bad at this.
Not at all. Everyone makes bugs, even expert programmers. A bug is just a mistake we can find and fix. Debugging is a normal, happy part of the work.
The character will fix its own mistake.
It will not. The computer does exactly what the blocks say, even if that is wrong. We have to find the wrong block and change it ourselves.
I must change lots of blocks to fix a bug.
Usually one small block is wrong. Change one thing, run it, and check — then change the next thing only if needed.
The green-flag block can go anywhere.
The Start on Green Flag block must sit at the top, or the blocks below it will not run when you tap the flag.
A character can have no blocks and simply stand still, like scenery. Only the characters we want to move need a program.

A bug is a mistake in a program. Finding and fixing it is called debugging. Everyone makes bugs — even the best programmers — so debugging is a normal, happy part of the job. And it is faster and easier with a friend: two pairs of eyes find the mistake sooner.

A bug is just a mistake in our instructions. When we find it and fix it, we are debugging. It is like proofreading a story to find the letter that is wrong.

project.title: Unit 6 Project: Be a Designer
project.brief: Bring together everything from Be a Designer into one finished piece of work you can show and explain.
steps: Plan first: write down what your be a designer project has to do before you build anything.
Build the smallest version that does one of those things, and run it.
Add one feature at a time, testing after each one.
When something breaks, change one thing, run it again, and note what fixed it.
Check your work against every success criterion below before you call it finished.
successCriteria: I planned my dance moves in order.
I built my dancer in ScratchJr.
I added a second dancer that joins in on a bump.
I found and fixed the bug with my partner.
I added one more block to make it better.
I tapped the green flag to check my dance.

selfAssessment: I can follow and understand an algorithm — a set of instructions in the correct order.
I can explain, in their own words, why the order of the steps matters.
I can plan instructions for a character by writing a simple dance algorithm.
I can turn an algorithm into a program in ScratchJr using blocks such as Start on Green Flag, Hop, Turn Right and Move Right.
I can add a second character that starts to dance using the Start on Bump block.
I can say what a bug is, and debug a short program by finding and fixing one mistake.
I can explain why it is helpful to work with others when debugging.
I can run a program with the green flag and check whether it did what they wanted.
